items.stem: Which of the following best describes "biodiversity"?
options: The variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in an area
The division of a continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches by human activities such as roads and farmland
A geologically short period in which a large proportion (over about 75 %) of species become extinct
The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations, including ecosystem, species and genetic diversity
items.answer: The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations, including ecosystem, species and genetic diversity
items.markingKey: D. "biodiversity" is the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations, including ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.

items.stem: "Biodiversity only refers to the number of species." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why Simpson’s reciprocal index is more informative than species richness alone.
items.answer: Richness counts species but ignores how individuals are distributed; the index includes evenness, so a community dominated by one species scores lower than one with equally common species, even with the same richness. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Richness counts species but ignores how individuals are distributed; the index includes evenness, so a community dominated by one species scores lower than one with equally common species, even with the same richness. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Simpson’s index for a coral reef fell from 8.2 to 3.1 after a bleaching event. Which is the best interpretation?
options: Diversity fell: fewer species and/or a few species now dominate.
items.answer: Diversity fell: fewer species and/or a few species now dominate.
items.markingKey: D. Lower D means lower richness and/or evenness.

items.stem:
Students sampled two areas of a stream in Scotland: area A (undisturbed) and area B (affected by pollution). The number of individuals of each species found is shown.

Species | Area A | Area B
mayfly nymphs | 8 | 3
caddisfly larvae | 9 | 86
freshwater shrimps | 13 | 1
stonefly nymphs | 20 | 6
water snails | 16 | 1

(a) State the species richness of each area. [1]
(b) Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index for area A. [2]
(c) Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index for area B. [2]
items.answer: (a) 5 species in each (b) 4.75 (c) 1.27

items.stem: Describe the three levels of biodiversity and explain how species diversity can be measured and compared.
items.answer: Ecosystem, species, genetic diversity with examples; richness and evenness; sampling (quadrats, nets); identification; Simpson’s reciprocal D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1); higher D = more diverse; comparison between sites/times; limitations – sampling effort, identification.
items.markingKey: Ecosystem, species, genetic diversity with examples; richness and evenness; sampling (quadrats, nets); identification; Simpson’s reciprocal D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1); higher D = more diverse; comparison between sites/times; limitations – sampling effort, identification.

items.stem: Define the term "ecosystem diversity".
items.answer: The variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in an area
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in an area. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The variety of alleles and genes within a species or population"?
items.answer: genetic diversity
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of genetic diversity.

items.stem: Distinguish between species richness and species evenness.
items.answer: Species richness is the number of species present; evenness is how equally individuals are distributed among those species.
items.markingKey: Species richness is the number of species present; evenness is how equally individuals are distributed among those species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is genetic diversity within a species important for its survival?
options: It provides variation on which natural selection can act if conditions change.
It reduces the number of alleles.
items.answer: It provides variation on which natural selection can act if conditions change.
items.markingKey: C. Low diversity increases vulnerability to disease and change.

items.stem: A sample from a stream in Scotland contained: mayfly nymphs 25, caddisfly larvae 31, freshwater shrimps 36, stonefly nymphs 29. Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index of diversity, D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1).
Outline one way in which the Amazon rainforest shows biodiversity at ecosystem, species and genetic levels.
items.answer: It contains around 10 % of known species and many unique habitats, from flooded várzea to terra firme forest. High ecosystem diversity supports enormous species richness, and each species contains genetic diversity adapted to local conditions.
items.markingKey: Context (It contains around 10 % of known species and many unique habitats, from flooded várzea to terra firme forest.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High ecosystem diversity supports enormous species richness, and each species contains genetic diversity adapted to local conditions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to biodiversity at ecosystem, species and genetic levels.

items.stem: A sample from a coral reef in the Red Sea contained 14 parrotfish, 21 damselfish and 15 butterflyfish. What is Simpson’s reciprocal index, D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1)?
A sample from leaf litter in a Costa Rican forest contained: ants 11, springtails 12, mites 11, beetles 26, woodlice 22. Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index of diversity, D = N(N − 1)/Σn(n − 1).
"Simpson’s reciprocal index is the best measure of the biodiversity of an area." Discuss.
items.answer: It is a useful, comparable measure of species diversity, but must be supplemented by measures of genetic and ecosystem diversity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it combines richness and evenness in one number that allows comparison between sites and over time; it is easy to calculate from sample counts. Arguments against: it does not measure genetic or ecosystem diversity; it depends on sampling method and on correct identification of species. Supported judgement: It is a useful, comparable measure of species diversity, but must be supplemented by measures of genetic and ecosystem diversity. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "invasive alien species"?
options: A species introduced by humans outside its natural range that spreads and harms native species or ecosystems
The normal rate at which species become extinct in the absence of mass extinction events
Harvesting a species faster than its population can recover, e.g. by overfishing or hunting
The variety of alleles and genes within a species or population
items.answer: A species introduced by humans outside its natural range that spreads and harms native species or ecosystems
items.markingKey: A. "invasive alien species" is a species introduced by humans outside its natural range that spreads and harms native species or ecosystems.

items.stem: Why does habitat fragmentation reduce biodiversity even if the total area remains large?
options: Edges are better habitats for all species.
Small isolated patches support smaller populations, which are more vulnerable and have less gene flow.
items.answer: Small isolated patches support smaller populations, which are more vulnerable and have less gene flow.
items.markingKey: D. Edge effects and isolation harm many species.

items.stem: Elena writes: "Planting large monoculture plantations restores biodiversity lost by deforestation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Monocultures such as oil palm support far fewer species than natural forest; they replace, not restore, the original ecosystem.
items.markingKey: Monocultures such as oil palm support far fewer species than natural forest; they replace, not restore, the original ecosystem. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: (final − initial)/initial × 100 = (19.4 − 32.1)/32.1 × 100 (M1) = -39.6 % (A1); sign/direction required.

items.stem: A WWF Living Planet Index report found an average decline of 69 % in monitored vertebrate populations between 1970 and 2018. If a population had 5000 individuals in 1970, about how many would remain after such a decline?
Using the extinction of the moa (Dinornithiformes) in New Zealand as an example, explain human causes of extinction.
items.answer: Nine species of large flightless birds were hunted to extinction within about 200 years of Polynesian settlement around 1300 CE. The birds had evolved without mammalian predators and reproduced slowly, so overhunting quickly eliminated them.
items.markingKey: Context (Nine species of large flightless birds were hunted to extinction within about 200 years of Polynesian settlement around 1300 CE.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The birds had evolved without mammalian predators and reproduced slowly, so overhunting quickly eliminated them. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to human causes of extinction.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Habitat destruction is a greater threat to biodiversity than climate change."
items.answer: Habitat destruction is the main current driver, but climate change is a growing threat and the two interact; both must be addressed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: land-use change is currently the largest driver of species loss; habitat loss directly removes populations and their resources. Arguments against: climate change is accelerating and may overtake habitat loss this century; climate change interacts with other threats, e.g. coral bleaching. Supported judgement: Habitat destruction is the main current driver, but climate change is a growing threat and the two interact; both must be addressed.

items.stem: Discuss the evidence that the Earth is experiencing a sixth mass extinction and outline its causes.
items.answer: Five past mass extinctions (Permian, K–Pg etc.) with natural causes; current extinction rate estimated 100–1000 × background; Living Planet Index declines (~69–73 %); IUCN Red List; causes: habitat loss (oil palm in Borneo), overexploitation (moa, passenger pigeon, overfishing), invasive species, pollution, climate change; evaluation: data uncertainty, many species undescribed.
items.markingKey: Five past mass extinctions (Permian, K–Pg etc.) with natural causes; current extinction rate estimated 100–1000 × background; Living Planet Index declines (~69–73 %); IUCN Red List; causes: habitat loss (oil palm in Borneo), overexploitation (moa, passenger pigeon, overfishing), invasive species, pollution, climate change; evaluation: data uncertainty, many species undescribed.

items.answer: Background extinction is the continuous low rate of species loss; mass extinction is a geologically brief event in which a large proportion of species disappear, far exceeding background rates.
items.markingKey: Background extinction is the continuous low rate of species loss; mass extinction is a geologically brief event in which a large proportion of species disappear, far exceeding background rates. items.stem: Briefly explain why evidence for the biodiversity crisis must come from reliable surveys.
items.answer: Population and species trends must be measured over time by repeatable methods (e.g. bird counts, camera traps, Living Planet Index); data from experts and citizen scientists must be verified; without reliable baselines declines cannot be quantified or compared.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Population and species trends must be measured over time by repeatable methods (e.g. bird counts, camera traps, Living Planet Index); data from experts and citizen scientists must be verified; without reliable baselines declines cannot be quantified or compared. items.stem: Why are island species especially vulnerable to invasive predators?
options: They often evolved without such predators and lack defensive behaviours.
items.answer: They often evolved without such predators and lack defensive behaviours.
items.markingKey: B. E.g. ground-nesting birds and introduced rats.

items.stem: Elena writes: "Extinctions only happened in the distant past, before humans." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many species have gone extinct due to humans, e.g. the moa, dodo and passenger pigeon, and current rates are far above background levels.
items.markingKey: Many species have gone extinct due to humans, e.g. the moa, dodo and passenger pigeon, and current rates are far above background levels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Students sampled two areas of a meadow in the Swiss Alps: area A (undisturbed) and area B (affected by pollution). The number of individuals of each species found is shown.

Species | Area A | Area B
meadow buttercup | 29 | 86
red clover | 8 | 8
yarrow | 30 | 7
oxeye daisy | 14 | 2
ribwort plantain | 5 | 5

(a) State the species richness of each area. [1]
(b) Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index for area A. [2]
(c) Calculate Simpson’s reciprocal index for area B. [2]
(d) Compare the diversity of the two areas and explain the difference using the data. [3]
items.answer: (a) 5 species in each (b) 3.77 (c) 1.56 (d) Area A is more diverse (D 3.77 vs 1.56); richness is the same, but area B is dominated by meadow buttercup, so its evenness is low.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 5 in each (A1). (b) [2] N = 86, N(N − 1) = 7310, Σn(n − 1) = 1940 (M1); D = 3.77 (A1). (c) [2] N = 108, N(N − 1) = 11556, Σn(n − 1) = 7430 (M1); D = 1.56 (A1). (d) [3] Correct comparison (A1); same richness, so difference due to evenness (R1); identifies dominant species (A1).

items.stem: Reintroducing grey wolves into Yellowstone National Park in 1995 is an example of
items.answer: rewilding
items.markingKey: C. Restoring a top predator restored trophic cascades.

items.stem: Why might conservationists prioritise evolutionarily distinct species?
options: Their loss would remove a large amount of unique evolutionary history.
They are easy to breed in zoos.
items.answer: Their loss would remove a large amount of unique evolutionary history.
items.markingKey: C. Phylogenetic diversity is irreplaceable.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ex situ conservation and in situ conservation.
items.answer: In situ conservation protects species within their natural habitats (e.g. reserves); ex situ conservation maintains them outside their habitats (zoos, botanic gardens, seed banks).
items.markingKey: In situ conservation protects species within their natural habitats (e.g. reserves); ex situ conservation maintains them outside their habitats (zoos, botanic gardens, seed banks). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Conservation should concentrate only on large, charismatic mammals." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Priority should be based on criteria such as threat, evolutionary distinctiveness and ecological role; many invertebrates, plants and amphibians are vital to ecosystems.
items.markingKey: Priority should be based on criteria such as threat, evolutionary distinctiveness and ecological role; many invertebrates, plants and amphibians are vital to ecosystems. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A critically endangered frog is threatened by chytrid fungus in its rainforest habitat. Which strategy combines ex situ and in situ approaches?
options: Storing frog seeds in a bank.
Captive breeding in a disease-free facility followed by reintroduction once the habitat is managed.
Removing all frogs from the wild permanently.
items.answer: Captive breeding in a disease-free facility followed by reintroduction once the habitat is managed.
items.markingKey: C. Combination protects the population while the threat is addressed.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Ex situ conservation is a waste of resources that should be spent on protecting habitats."
items.answer: Both approaches are needed: habitat protection is the priority, but ex situ conservation is a vital safety net for critically endangered species.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: without protected habitats, captive species cannot be reintroduced; ex situ programmes are expensive per species. Arguments against: some species (e.g. California condor, Przewalski’s horse) survived only because of captive breeding; seed banks are cheap insurance for genetic diversity. Supported judgement: Both approaches are needed: habitat protection is the priority, but ex situ conservation is a vital safety net for critically endangered species.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Conservation of species outside their natural habitats, such as in zoos, botanic gardens or seed banks"?
items.answer: ex situ conservation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of ex situ conservation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why rewilding can restore biodiversity in an ecosystem.
items.answer: Reintroduced keystone species such as wolves or beavers restore interactions (e.g. predation, habitat engineering) that regulate other populations; this creates trophic cascades, more varied habitats and allows natural processes to increase species diversity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reintroduced keystone species such as wolves or beavers restore interactions (e.g. predation, habitat engineering) that regulate other populations; this creates trophic cascades, more varied habitats and allows natural processes to increase species diversity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is a limitation of seed banks?
options: They are a form of in situ conservation.
Seeds cannot be stored for more than a year.
Stored seeds do not evolve in response to environmental change and some seeds cannot be dried.
items.answer: Stored seeds do not evolve in response to environmental change and some seeds cannot be dried.
items.markingKey: C. Recalcitrant seeds (e.g. many tropical trees) cannot be banked.

items.stem: A student claims: "Zoos alone can save endangered species from extinction." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Zoos can maintain populations, but unless habitats are protected and threats removed, species cannot be returned to the wild; in situ conservation is essential.
items.markingKey: Zoos can maintain populations, but unless habitats are protected and threats removed, species cannot be returned to the wild; in situ conservation is essential. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the EDGE of Existence programme’s work on the Chinese giant salamander shows prioritisation of species for conservation.
items.answer: The salamander, among the most evolutionarily distinct amphibians, is critically endangered by overharvesting for food. High ED and GE scores focus funding on a species whose loss would remove a unique lineage.
items.markingKey: Context (The salamander, among the most evolutionarily distinct amphibians, is critically endangered by overharvesting for food.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Outline one way in which the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway shows ex situ conservation.
items.answer: The vault stores over a million seed samples of crop varieties at −18 °C inside a mountain. It preserves genetic diversity of crops as insurance against loss in the field, though stored seeds do not evolve.
items.markingKey: Context (The vault stores over a million seed samples of crop varieties at −18 °C inside a mountain.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It preserves genetic diversity of crops as insurance against loss in the field, though stored seeds do not evolve. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ex situ conservation.

items.stem: "Extinctions only happened in the distant past, before humans." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many species have gone extinct due to humans, e.g. the moa, dodo and passenger pigeon, and current rates are far above background levels.
items.markingKey: Many species have gone extinct due to humans, e.g. the moa, dodo and passenger pigeon, and current rates are far above background levels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Simpson’s reciprocal index is the best measure of the biodiversity of an area."
items.answer: It is a useful, comparable measure of species diversity, but must be supplemented by measures of genetic and ecosystem diversity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it combines richness and evenness in one number that allows comparison between sites and over time; it is easy to calculate from sample counts. Arguments against: it does not measure genetic or ecosystem diversity; it depends on sampling method and on correct identification of species. Supported judgement: It is a useful, comparable measure of species diversity, but must be supplemented by measures of genetic and ecosystem diversity.

items.stem: "Ex situ conservation is a waste of resources that should be spent on protecting habitats." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Both approaches are needed: habitat protection is the priority, but ex situ conservation is a vital safety net for critically endangered species.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: without protected habitats, captive species cannot be reintroduced; ex situ programmes are expensive per species. Arguments against: some species (e.g. California condor, Przewalski’s horse) survived only because of captive breeding; seed banks are cheap insurance for genetic diversity. Supported judgement: Both approaches are needed: habitat protection is the priority, but ex situ conservation is a vital safety net for critically endangered species. items.stem: "Habitat destruction is a greater threat to biodiversity than climate change." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Habitat destruction is the main current driver, but climate change is a growing threat and the two interact; both must be addressed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mass extinction"?
options: Conservation of species outside their natural habitats, such as in zoos, botanic gardens or seed banks
A species that is both Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered, prioritised for conservation by the EDGE of Existence programme
A geologically short period in which a large proportion (over about 75 %) of species become extinct
Restoring an ecosystem by reintroducing missing species (e.g. top predators) and allowing natural processes to resume
items.answer: A geologically short period in which a large proportion (over about 75 %) of species become extinct
items.markingKey: C. "mass extinction" is a geologically short period in which a large proportion (over about 75 %) of species become extinct.

items.stem: Which level of biodiversity is reduced when a population loses alleles through inbreeding?
items.answer: genetic diversity
items.markingKey: C. Small populations lose alleles by drift and inbreeding.

items.stem: What does the EDGE of Existence programme prioritise?
items.answer: species that are evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered
items.markingKey: species that are evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered. Such species represent large amounts of unique evolutionary history.

items.stem: "Planting large monoculture plantations restores biodiversity lost by deforestation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Monocultures such as oil palm support far fewer species than natural forest; they replace, not restore, the original ecosystem.
items.markingKey: Monocultures such as oil palm support far fewer species than natural forest; they replace, not restore, the original ecosystem. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Elena writes: "Biodiversity only refers to the number of species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Zoos alone can save endangered species from extinction." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Zoos can maintain populations, but unless habitats are protected and threats removed, species cannot be returned to the wild; in situ conservation is essential.
items.markingKey: Zoos can maintain populations, but unless habitats are protected and threats removed, species cannot be returned to the wild; in situ conservation is essential. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mass extinction and background extinction.
items.answer: Background extinction is the continuous low rate of species loss; mass extinction is a geologically brief event in which a large proportion of species disappear, far exceeding background rates.
items.markingKey: Background extinction is the continuous low rate of species loss; mass extinction is a geologically brief event in which a large proportion of species disappear, far exceeding background rates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between species evenness and species richness.
items.answer: Species richness is the number of species present; evenness is how equally individuals are distributed among those species.
items.markingKey: Species richness is the number of species present; evenness is how equally individuals are distributed among those species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is in situ conservation generally preferred to ex situ conservation?
options: Species remain in their natural ecosystem, maintaining interactions and natural selection.
items.answer: Species remain in their natural ecosystem, maintaining interactions and natural selection.
items.markingKey: D. Whole ecosystems are protected.
